title: XCENA MX1 CXL Computational Memory Device at Hot Chips 2026 with Samsung
gist: XCENA's MX1 CXL computational memory device pairs 3,072 custom RISC-V cores with SSD-backed 'Infinite Memory' and Samsung's rack-scale CXL pooling to argue that AI workloads bottleneck on memory capacity/bandwidth/power before compute, showing large efficiency and throughput gains in RAG search and LLM decode benchmarks.

insights.claim: XCENA's core thesis is that AI workloads stall on memory capacity, bandwidth, and power efficiency before they stall on raw compute, motivating a computational-memory device (MX1) rather than a faster host processor or GPU.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reinforces the broader industry narrative that memory bandwidth, not FLOPS, is the binding constraint for LLM inference — favoring memory-centric silicon and CXL-based architectures over raw GPU compute scaling.

insights.claim: The article frames XCENA and Samsung's joint pitch as concrete evidence that the AI/analytics memory bottleneck can be solved inside a CXL device rather than by adding a larger host CPU or a faster GPU.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If this thesis holds industry-wide, CXL memory-expansion and computational-memory vendors (XCENA, Samsung, Marvell, Astera Labs) capture value that would otherwise accrue to GPU vendors for memory-bound inference workloads.

themes.theme: MX1 architecture: many simple RISC-V cores

insights.claim: XCENA built MX1 on Samsung Foundry's 4nm process with 24 subsystems of four clusters each holding 32 memory units (MUs), totaling 3,072 custom RISC-V cores, with each subsystem acting as an independent host job allocation unit sharing a 128MB L3 cache.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Confirms Samsung Foundry as a beneficiary of the computational-memory trend, and validates RISC-V as the ISA of choice for near-memory compute at scale.

insights.claim: XCENA chose many simple in-order RISC-V cores over fewer large cores because target workloads (in-memory analytics, RAG retrieval, memory compression) are bandwidth-bound and power-sensitive, and the open ISA provides a mature toolchain plus room for custom data-parallel instructions.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A reusable design framework: bandwidth-bound, power-sensitive workloads favor many-simple-core near-memory architectures over few-large-core designs — applicable when evaluating other computational-memory or PIM entrants.

insights.claim: MX1 includes a Vector Processing Engine delivering roughly 3 TFLOPS of peak dot-product throughput per SoC, targeting RAG vector search and KV cache scoring via per-MU command queues.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Purpose-built vector compute embedded in memory directly targets the RAG/vector-search market segment, a growing enterprise AI workload category.

insights.claim: MX1 uses a single virtual address space shared between host and memory units, letting existing malloc-based code move to CXL memory with minimal changes while a CXL-aware allocator maintains per-tenant page tables for isolation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Lowers the software integration barrier for adopting computational memory, which is often the real obstacle to novel memory architectures gaining developer traction.
insights.locator: Host and MU share one virtual address space

themes.theme: Performance and efficiency benchmarks vs. host/DRAM

insights.claim: XCENA reports MX1 analytics kernel throughput up to 4.7x versus host-over-CXL and 2x versus local DRAM, at roughly a quarter of host power, yielding efficiency gains up to 18.7x versus CXL and 6.2x versus DRAM, benchmarked on an Intel Xeon 6767P reference system excluding idle power.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Large vendor-reported efficiency multiples (up to ~19x) are a strong claim that would materially undercut CPU-centric analytics infrastructure costs if validated independently.
insights.locator: More throughput at lower power – analytics kernels

insights.claim: XCENA's 'Infinite Memory' feature presents SSD capacity as byte-addressable CXL memory using a DRAM-plus-NAND hybrid where DRAM caches 64KB SSD pages tracked by a 1024-entry map cache TLB, with misses filled by firmware on the MU cores.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is a modern echo of Intel Optane-style memory tiering (explicitly noted by the author), suggesting a market opening for SSD-backed memory expansion now that Optane is discontinued.
insights.locator: Presenting SSD capacity as byte-addressable CXL memory

insights.claim: In KV cache tests with a pinned prefix resident in Infinite Memory, query time-to-first-token tracks DRAM at just 1.13x; dropping the pin raises that to 1.57x, and a raw SSD baseline reaches 1.86x, with lookahead prefetching approaching near-DRAM performance — tested on Llama-3.1-8B with vLLM, LMCache, and an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Pro.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows SSD-backed KV cache tiering can approach DRAM-level latency for LLM serving, a potential cost-reduction lever for inference providers facing HBM/DRAM scarcity.
insights.locator: Infinite Memory applied to KV cache

themes.theme: Samsung rack-scale CXL pooling and hyperscaler adoption

insights.claim: Samsung stated on stage that CXL is being adopted by all major hyperscalers for use cases like databases and AI/KV cache, contrasting DDR5 bandwidth (268.8 GB/s) against a 64GB/s PCIe Gen6 x8 host link to justify computing in place rather than moving data to the host.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A direct hyperscaler-adoption data point for CXL, useful for tracking whether CXL moves from niche to mainstream data center memory architecture.

insights.claim: Samsung and XCENA's reference rack-scale system pairs a Liqid CXL switch with GPU servers using 96GB NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell parts, targeting 20TB of pooled memory capacity at 2.7TB/s of bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Concrete rack-scale spec target signals Samsung/XCENA are building toward production-grade CXL memory pooling appliances, not just research prototypes — a competitive data point against other CXL pooling vendors.

insights.claim: Samsung's NDC (near-data-computing) API is vendor-agnostic and open-sourced through OCP FTI DCC, with PyTorch integration routed through OpenXLA and PrivateUse1 so AI frameworks can reach XCENA's PXL library without code changes.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: An open, standardized software layer lowers switching costs and could let Samsung's near-memory compute ecosystem scale across multiple hardware vendors beyond just XCENA.
insights.locator: Samsung-XCENA SW Runtime Approach for PNM: NDC API

insights.claim: Samsung's RAG vector search benchmark using 10 processing-near-memory (PNM) devices with FAISS IVF Flat indexing over a 512M-vector Laion 5B index delivered 64x higher queries-per-second and 65x better queries-per-energy than a host CPU with a CXL memory pool.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 64x QPS improvement for RAG vector search is a striking efficiency claim that, if reproducible, could reshape cost structures for large-scale retrieval-augmented generation deployments.
insights.locator: AI Use Case 1 – RAG Vector Search on CXL-PNM

insights.claim: In Samsung's GPU+PNM hybrid attention decode test at 100K context length using LLaMA-3.1-70B INT8 across two servers (each with five MX1 devices and NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPUs), throughput rose 3.35x (17.7 vs 5.50 tokens/sec) and token-per-energy rose 3.84x (4.31 vs 1.12 tokens/kJ) versus GPU-only attention.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is presented as the 'headline number' of the session — a concrete demonstration that offloading long-context attention to near-memory compute can meaningfully cut GPU energy cost per token, a direct economic lever for inference providers at long context lengths.
insights.locator: AI Use Case 2 – LLM Decode: GPU + PNM Hybrid Attention

insights.claim: In the hybrid decode architecture, hit pages stay on the GPU while miss pages route to the PNM device, which returns only the computed attention result rather than shipping the full KV pages back to the GPU, reducing data movement overhead.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This compute-near-data pattern (return only the result, not the raw data) is a generalizable architectural principle for reducing memory-bandwidth pressure in disaggregated inference systems.
insights.locator: AI Use Case 2 – LLM Decode: GPU + PNM Hybrid Attention

insights.claim: The author notes the timing of the Gen6 x8 PCIe host-link comparison in Samsung's slides gives away that server CPUs supporting PCIe Gen6 are only just beginning to launch, suggesting these products are being benchmarked against near-term rather than currently shipping infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A subtle timing tell that Samsung/XCENA's benchmarks are forward-looking relative to actual deployed server CPU generations, relevant for assessing how soon these products could see real-world hyperscaler deployment.
